summary: The note surveys how weather drives seasonal patterns of utility outages, with dated examples from winter snowstorms and burst water mains, autumn hurricanes and windstorms, and spring and summer thunderstorms and heat waves. It then describes utility, community, business, and government responses, including predictive analytics, infrastructure hardening, emergency distribution, backup power, and federal grants. It closes by pointing to smart grids, renewables, and battery storage as future resilience measures.
one_line: Weather-related utility outages follow seasonal patterns, and utilities, communities, businesses, and governments respond with forecasting, hardening, community aid, and policy.
key_facts: On October 15, a snowstorm in Vermont caused power outages affecting approximately 50,000 residents; Jennifer Grayson of Vermont Electrical Services blamed heavy snow and ice snapping tree branches onto power lines.

On November 12, a rapid temperature drop burst water mains in Saint Paul, Minnesota, disrupting water to over 10,000 homes and businesses; city official Mark Svenson cited extreme cold straining aging infrastructure.
On September 30, 2023, Hurricane Elara struck the Carolinas and left over 200,000 residents without power.
Lineman Jameson Briggs said downed trees over power lines and flooded substations hinder swift power restoration after hurricanes.
On October 25, windstorms in the Pacific Northwest caused outages in Washington State, with fallen trees cutting power to 70,000 residents in Seattle.
Seattle City Light spokesperson Angela Montez said the city's vast tree canopy poses a considerable risk during severe windstorms.
On May 5, 2024, a supercell thunderstorm in Oklahoma caused outages lasting several days; Heartland Electric documented more than 500 lightning strikes affecting the grid.
Jennifer Clarke of the National Weather Service said summer heat waves increase air conditioning use, which can overload and collapse the power grid.

Utilities use predictive analytics to preemptively mobilize crews, as seen in restoration after Hurricane Elara, and invest in hardening such as stronger poles, underground cabling, and automatic switchgear.
In Saint Paul, officials swiftly set up emergency water distribution centers after the main breaks, and Seattle volunteers cleared debris during the October windstorms.
GlobalTech Solutions, whose CEO is Linda Chang, invested in backup power systems and satellite communications to keep operations running during outages.
After Hurricane Elara, federal grants were allocated to rebuild and improve electrical infrastructure.
Smart grids with machine learning, renewable energy, and battery storage are expected to improve future resilience.
